subject: Psychology
name: Psychology, Units 3 and 4
about: VCE, Nervous system, learning, memory, sleep and wellbeing
syllabus: VCE Psychology Study Design (from 2023), Units 3 and 4

units.title: Unit 3: How does experience affect behaviour and mental processes?

points.title: Central and peripheral nervous systems
points.brief: The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord. The peripheral nervous system carries messages between them and the rest of the body.

points.title: Somatic and autonomic nervous systems
points.brief: The somatic system carries sensory messages in and voluntary movement messages out. The autonomic system runs organs and glands without conscious effort.

points.title: Sympathetic and parasympathetic
points.brief: The sympathetic nervous system readies the body for action, raising heart rate and breathing. The parasympathetic system calms it and keeps it steady.

points.title: Conscious and unconscious responses
points.brief: A conscious response involves awareness and choice. An unconscious response, such as a spinal reflex, happens before the brain is aware of the stimulus.

points.title: The spinal reflex
points.brief: A sensory neuron passes a signal to an interneuron in the spinal cord, which signals a motor neuron, so the body pulls away from danger before the brain registers pain.

points.title: Neurotransmitters at the synapse
points.brief: A neuron releases neurotransmitters across the synaptic gap to receptors on the next neuron. Glutamate is excitatory and GABA is inhibitory.

points.title: Neuromodulators
points.brief: Neuromodulators such as dopamine and serotonin act on many neurons at once, changing how they respond. Dopamine links to reward and movement, serotonin to mood and sleep.

points.title: Synaptic plasticity
points.brief: Synapses change with use. Long-term potentiation strengthens a connection that is used often; long-term depression weakens one that is not. Sprouting, rerouting and pruning also reshape them.

points.title: Stress and stressors
points.brief: Stress is a state of psychological and physiological arousal from a stressor. Stressors can be internal, such as worry, or external, such as an exam.

points.title: Fight, flight or freeze
points.brief: An acute stress response in which the sympathetic system prepares the body to fight, run, or freeze to avoid notice.

points.title: Cortisol
points.brief: Cortisol is a stress hormone that keeps energy available during a long stressor, but staying high for a long time weakens the immune system.

points.title: General adaptation syndrome
points.brief: Selye's model of the body's stress response over time, alarm reaction (shock, then countershock), resistance, then exhaustion.

points.title: The transactional model of stress
points.brief: Lazarus and Folkman's model says stress depends on how a person appraises a stressor and their resources to cope, in primary and secondary appraisal.

points.title: The gut-brain axis
points.brief: The gut and brain send signals both ways through the vagus nerve and gut microbes. Stress can change gut microbes, and gut health can affect mood.

points.title: Approach and avoidance coping
points.brief: Approach strategies deal with the stressor directly. Avoidance strategies keep away from it, which can help briefly but often leaves the problem in place.

points.title: Coping flexibility
points.brief: Coping flexibility is noticing when a strategy is not working and switching to another. A strategy that helps in one situation may not in another.

points.title: Classical conditioning
points.brief: A neutral stimulus paired with an unconditioned stimulus comes to cause a conditioned response, in three phases (before, during and after conditioning).

points.title: Operant conditioning
points.brief: Learning by consequences in a three-phase model, antecedent, behaviour, consequence. Reinforcement makes a behaviour more likely; punishment makes it less likely.

points.title: Positive and negative reinforcement
points.brief: Positive reinforcement adds something pleasant. Negative reinforcement takes away something unpleasant. Both make a behaviour more likely, unlike punishment.

points.title: Observational learning
points.brief: Learning by watching a model, in five steps, attention, retention, reproduction, motivation and reinforcement.

points.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander ways of knowing
points.brief: Learning that is multimodal, connected to Country, passed on through story, song and practice, and tied to relationships and place.

points.title: The multi-store model
points.brief: Atkinson and Shiffrin's model has sensory memory, short-term memory and long-term memory, each with its own capacity and duration.

points.title: Explicit and implicit memory
points.brief: Explicit memories are recalled on purpose, such as facts and events. Implicit memories show in what we do without trying, such as skills and conditioned responses.

points.title: Episodic and semantic memory
points.brief: Episodic memory holds personal events with a time and place. Semantic memory holds general facts and knowledge.

points.title: Brain areas in memory
points.brief: The hippocampus forms explicit memories, the amygdala adds emotion, the neocortex stores them, and the basal ganglia and cerebellum handle implicit memory.

points.title: Autobiographical memory and imagining the future
points.brief: Recalling personal events and imagining future ones use the same episodic and semantic systems, so loss of one often affects the other.

points.title: Alzheimer's disease and memory
points.brief: Alzheimer's disease damages neurons through amyloid plaques and tangles, and episodic memory is often lost first.

points.title: Aphantasia
points.brief: Aphantasia is being unable to picture images in the mind. People with it can still remember facts, but often recall past events with less detail.

points.title: Mnemonics
points.brief: Memory aids such as acronyms, acrostics and the method of loci link new information to cues that are easier to recall.

points.title: Sung narratives and songlines
points.brief: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have long kept knowledge in songs, stories and places along Country, which works as a powerful memory system.

units.title: Unit 4: How is mental wellbeing supported and maintained?

points.title: Sleep as a state of consciousness
points.brief: Sleep is a naturally occurring altered state of consciousness, with less awareness of surroundings and changes in brain activity.

points.title: NREM and REM sleep
points.brief: NREM sleep has stages that get deeper, with slower brain waves. REM sleep has fast brain waves, rapid eye movements, little muscle tone and vivid dreams.

points.title: Measuring sleep
points.brief: The EEG records brain waves, the EMG muscle activity and the EOG eye movements. Sleep diaries and video monitoring add what the person and an observer see.

points.title: Circadian and ultradian rhythms
points.brief: The sleep-wake cycle follows a circadian rhythm of about 24 hours. Cycles of NREM and REM sleep through the night are ultradian rhythms.

points.title: Melatonin and the SCN
points.brief: The suprachiasmatic nucleus responds to light and tells the pineal gland when to release melatonin, which makes us sleepy.

points.title: Sleep across the lifespan
points.brief: Total sleep and the share of REM sleep fall from infancy to old age. Adolescents' sleep timing shifts later.

points.title: Partial sleep deprivation
points.brief: Too little sleep affects mood, thinking and reactions. Staying awake 17 hours affects a person about as much as a blood alcohol level of 0.05.

points.title: Circadian rhythm sleep disorders
points.brief: Delayed sleep phase syndrome and shift work disorder put sleep out of step with daily life, causing tiredness and poor functioning.

points.title: Improving sleep
points.brief: Bright light therapy and zeitgebers such as daylight, temperature and meal times help reset the body clock. Sleep hygiene builds habits that support good sleep.

points.title: The mental wellbeing continuum
points.brief: Mental wellbeing ranges from mentally healthy, through a mental health problem, to a mental health disorder, and a person can move along it.

points.title: Ways of describing mental wellbeing
points.brief: Mental wellbeing can be shown by high levels of functioning, resilience, and social and emotional wellbeing.

points.title: Social and emotional wellbeing
points.brief: For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, wellbeing connects body, mind, family, community, culture, Country and spirituality.

points.title: Stress, anxiety and phobia compared
points.brief: Stress responds to a stressor and passes. Anxiety continues after the stressor or without one. A phobia is an intense, irrational fear of something specific.

points.title: Protective factors for wellbeing
points.brief: Good food, enough sleep, coping and mindfulness strategies, and support from family, friends and community help keep mental wellbeing high.

points.title: Cultural determinants of wellbeing
points.brief: For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, self-determination and connection to culture, Country and community support social and emotional wellbeing.

points.title: Biological factors in specific phobia
points.brief: Low GABA activity and long-term potentiation that strengthens a fear response can help a specific phobia develop and stay.

points.title: Psychological factors in specific phobia
points.brief: Phobias can be learned by classical conditioning and kept by operant conditioning when avoiding the feared thing brings relief. Catastrophic thinking feeds them.

points.title: Social factors in specific phobia
points.brief: A frightening event, learning fear from others, and stigma around seeking help can all add to a specific phobia.

points.title: Evidence-based treatments for phobia
points.brief: Treatments include CBT, systematic desensitisation (gradual exposure while relaxed), breathing retraining, exercise and, briefly, medication such as benzodiazepines.

points.title: Types of investigations
points.brief: Psychology uses controlled experiments, correlational studies, case studies, fieldwork, literature reviews and simulations, each suited to different questions.

points.title: Validity
points.brief: Internal validity asks whether a study measured what it set out to. External validity asks whether its results apply beyond the sample.

points.title: Accuracy, precision, repeatability and reproducibility
points.brief: Accuracy is closeness to the true value. Precision is closeness of results to each other. Repeatability and reproducibility ask whether the same result comes again.

points.title: Representing and judging data
points.brief: Tables and graphs show patterns, and conclusions should only claim what the data supports, noting outliers and limits.

points.title: Ethical concepts
points.brief: Research is judged by integrity, justice, beneficence, non-maleficence and respect, beside the ethical guidelines for participants.
